summary:
No local Ulsan ordinance, directive or enforcement practice concerning trans people is documented in the available sources; the national framework governs the city directly. South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and legal gender recognition is available without a surgical prerequisite: on 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved registered-sex change from male to female for five applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that gender change cannot be determined by surgery, that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are reference material rather than criteria, and that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity.

Trans visitors hold a judicially enforced right to public restrooms nationwide. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, ruling that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The judgment binds police practice in Ulsan as elsewhere.

The same reporting records the practical gap between that ruling and daily conduct. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink outlets, and 36% went without restroom use. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.

Broader conditions still shape the visit. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds; organised conservative opposition remains active; and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people while noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, though the Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling extended recognition of same-sex partners' healthcare rights in that specific area.
tangentialFactors:
The military exception is the one place where conduct is criminalised: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 punishes consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether. Ulsan hosts significant naval and industrial military installations, so this framework is geographically proximate even though it binds service members rather than civilian visitors.

In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult. A visitor needing inpatient care should expect no written institutional standard on the point.

Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are described as broadly positive, which sets Ulsan apart: the city has no comparable documented district, so the surrounding context of active conservative opposition and absent statutory protection carries more weight there than in the capital.
localsOnly:
Residents can change registered sex in the family relations register without having undergone sex-reassignment surgery, following the May 2024 Yeongdong ruling, and the Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the register.

The restroom judgment is available to residents as well as visitors: police advice to avoid a facility of the acquired gender is actionable as an infringement of personal rights, with damages awarded against the state, and the appellate court's characterisation of comfortable restroom use as a fundamental and universal human right applies to schools, academies and private premises in the reasoning used against the beauty academy in Pohang.

Residents nonetheless report avoidance behaviour at scale, per the 2021 survey of 591 transgender respondents, and employment, services and accommodation offer no statutory recourse on grounds of gender identity in the absence of an anti-discrimination law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Ulsan metropolitan police have issued any internal instruction following the July 2024 appellate judgment is unresolved; the sources establish that the ruling binds police practice nationally but contain no Ulsan-specific reporting.

The Yeongdong and Pohang rulings are regional court decisions outside Ulsan, applied here as national precedent; whether any Ulsan district court has ruled on registered-sex change or facility access is not sourced.

The 2021 National Human Rights Commission survey figures are reported second-hand through Korea Times coverage rather than from the commission's own publication, and the underlying methodology is not available in these sources.

No source documents hate-crime incidents, partner recognition for foreign visitors, or entry and visa screening of trans travellers in Ulsan; the absence of documentation is not evidence of absence.
